clusters.name: Stepfather arrives, sister born, chess anxiety, 1987
clusters.reason: Around the time your stepfather settled into the family and your sister was born, you were clashing with him while staying close to your dad, and you made the chess squad but felt out of your depth. Your anxiety rose as family membership shifted.

clusters.name: Left home, wrist injury, grandfather died, 1989–1992
clusters.reason: You went to the conservatory in 1991 and leaned hard on your closest friend, but when you hurt your wrist weeks later you couldn't play and you two fell apart. Around the same time your grandfather died and your mother remarried; you were lost and low, getting high, unable to get going. Your grandmother was treated for thyroid cancer. By early 1992 you were at community college in a bleak state, days asleep and nights out playing pool, but by 1994 an exchange abroad steadied you and you raced through your degree.
clusters.change: The core of the period is your first term away from home: you hurt your wrist, your closest friendship broke under the strain, and your grandfather died within months, leaving you without footing. Your mother's remarriage that autumn added to the shift in who was around you. The period settles once you found your drive again through the exchange and coursework.

clusters.name: Performing peak, insomnia, breakup, therapy, 1998–1999
clusters.reason: You played the best you ever had and won competitions, but insomnia began getting in the way before concerts though you practised hard. Within a year you and Joelle separated, and you started with a therapist after the split, reading about family patterns like your grandfather's gambling.

clusters.name: Burned out performing, grandmother dying, moved away, depression, 2001–2004
clusters.reason: You ran out of steam for performing and were less content by the month. Your grandmother was found to have bowel cancer and underwent operations and chemotherapy around the same time. You had a disastrous audition for the national orchestra in your home town and were done with performing. You were on poor terms with family and friends and left Thornbury for Gull Harbour, then met Marisol and moved to Fenwick with her. When you split within the year you sank into a deep depression back in Thornbury, hardly moving from the sofa. You avoided your family, relied on friends instead, and your dad and a friend talked several times about you. By early 2004 you began swimming laps, asked your parents for help with therapy costs, and returned to your therapist. Your grandmother died that February. Within months you found direction toward nursing.
clusters.change: The period runs from your burnout through your grandmother's death. It opens with you running out of steam for performing and her cancer diagnosis around the same time, and settles once you returned to therapy and began to climb out of the depression, finding a path forward.

clusters.name: Grandmother and grandfather died, mother pushed for visit, cutoff, 2008
clusters.reason: Your grandmother died in January 2008 and your grandfather around the same time. In summer you went to build at Alder Creek with Silas, but you were too drained for conversation with your mother. She pressed you to visit despite your repeated refusals and the visit went wrong; you kept the door shut on her. When you left for nursing school in Marlow Sound that August you stopped speaking to her, a silence that held for roughly a year. Around the same time your aunt had a stroke.

clusters.name: Married, sister pregnant, wife's family close, sleep worsens, 2017–2019
clusters.reason: You married Wren in spring 2017 and saw your mother a bit less once she came along. Your cousin Alice was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis that October, and your other aunt's memory was slipping. Your sister Tara married and was expecting your father's first grandchild. Your wife's brother Leo moved back nearby in 2019 with his young family. Around that time your job steadied and your anxiety eased, but you also felt constantly driven to push projects forward and started a sleeping pill. In October 2019 your wife was swamped by back-to-back events, and you overfunctioned laying out a plan to settle her. Her family—father, brother, and she—talk all day and nothing happens to one that the others don't hear. At the family gathering at the lake for her mother's retirement you were awake from the small hours with no more sleep and could only pull back as others rose; you felt you didn't belong. Your wife was anxious when you'd had no sleep at family occasions and there were long quiet drives home.
clusters.change: The period opens with your marriage and tightens around late 2019 when your wife's family obligations piled up and her close-knit family system was on full display. Your sleep pattern worsened at family gatherings, and you found yourself overfunctioning to manage her overwhelm. The events settle by late October as immediate pressures eased, though the underlying patterns with her family remain.

periods.name: year I left home
periods.words: The first is the year I left home: I went off to the conservatory, hurt my wrist in the first term and couldn't play, dropped out and drifted at my mother's place, then spent a bleak spell at the community college shooting pool every night until an exchange in Portugal snapped me out of it and I tore through the rest of my coursework.

periods.name: long slump
periods.words: The second is the long slump, roughly ages 27 to 29, when nothing at home felt right, I moved to Gull Harbour away from nearly everyone I knew, then followed Marisol to Fenwick, and when that fell apart I went under, a depression I only really climbed out of after nursing school.
